messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Perhaps this question has been answered before but I trying to find out how to handle the following case.

parcels come in during the day and the warehouse closes at 18:00
if a parcel is being processed at 18:00 by a resource then processing should complete. Other packages that have arrived before 18:00 should not handled anymore on the same day.
if a higher priority parcel comes in before 18:00 then that parcel preempts the parcel which is currently being processed.

Now there are some setups, each with different behavior:
add_resource with preemption FALSE with a schedule: Parcels that are processed at 18:00 will continue processing until finished, but they will not be preempted by a higher prio package that came in just before 18:00
add_resource with preemption TRUE with a schedule: High prio parcels will preempt parcels with lower priority, but processing will stop at exactly 18:00.
add_resource with preemption FALSE and a separate task of high prio that will capture the resource at 18:00. This will lead to the parcel to finish processing, but also all other parcels that arrived before 18:00 will be processed. Then, after that, the high prio task will seize the resource.
Option 3 is almost there, but how do I prevent other parcels that are not being processed at 18:00 and that arrived before 18:00 from being processed?

Cheers
  Erik

messages.body_plain:
I think I might not have answered my original question. I am now defining the resource as preemptive and using the 'premptive' option in the add_generator call to make sure that only priority customers can preempt customers and that the timeout logic does not preempt.

This should lead to the situation where a high priority customer (priority=10) is immediately handled, even when that requires handling after the normal closing hours (18:00). Then the closing trajectory which has higher priority (priority=5) than the normal customer (priority=0) should take over, causing the closing of the bank and the continued handling of the customer the next day. However, what I am seeing is that the original low prio customer is preempted by the high prio customer. Then the low prio customer is handled, and after that the bank is closed. Is this the expected behavior?

Here is the code:

resources = c("counter")
capacities = c(1)

env = simmer("bank")
for (i in seq_along(resources)) {

  env = env %>% add_resource(resources[[i]], preemptive=TRUE, capacity = capacities[[i]])

}

customer =
  trajectory("customer") %>%
  log_("Entering") %>%
  set_attribute("t0", function() now(env)) %>%
  seize("counter", 1) %>%
  set_attribute("t1", function() now(env) - get_attribute(env, "t0"), mod = "+") %>%
  log_("being served") %>%
  timeout(5) %>%
  release("counter") %>%
  log_("leaving")

openResources = function(resources, capacities) {
  traj = trajectory("open resources")
  for (i in seq_along(resources)) {
    resource = resources[[i]]
    capacity = capacities[[i]]
    traj = traj %>%
      log_(paste("Opening", resource, "capacity", capacity, "\n")) %>%
      set_capacity(resource, capacity)
  }
  traj
}

closeResources = function(resources) {
  # closing resources in parallel so that closing will start for
  # all resources at the same time.
  closeResourceTrajectory = function(resource) {
    trajectory(paste("close", resource)) %>%
      log_(paste("closing", resource)) %>%
      seize(resource, function() get_capacity(env, resource)) %>%
      log_(paste("closed", resource)) %>%
      set_capacity(resource, 0) %>%
      release_all(resource)
  }

  args = lapply(resources, function(resource) {
    closeResourceTrajectory(resource)
  })
  trajectory("close resource") %>%
    do_parallel(args, .env = env, wait = TRUE)
}

bank = env %>%

  add_generator("customer", customer, at(17, 17.5), mon=2, preemptible = 10) %>%
  add_generator("priority_customer", customer, at(17.75), mon = 2,
               priority = 11, preemptible = 20) %>%
  add_generator("closing", closeResources(resources),
                from_to(18, 100, function() 24), priority = 5) %>%

  add_generator("opening", openResources(resources, capacities),

                from_to(7, 100, function() 24), priority = 5)

bank %>% run(until = 100)

Also, perhaps this is getting too complicated and it would be better to add two closing generators: one at the exact closing time that does not preempt the customer (priority=5) and one 3 hours after that with a high priority (priority=30) that makes sure that the resources are closed. That would represent a more realistic case where the employee would refuse to do more than 3 hours of overtime.

What do you think? I am just exploring the possibilities here.

It is. By default, preempted customers eventually finish their work,
and for that effect, they are handled in a special queue, different
from the main one. If you want to override this behaviour, you need to
set the queue_size_strict parameter to TRUE. Note that, in this way,
preemption may cause rejection (if there is no space left in the
regular queue).

For this problem you are describing, consider increasing the priority
of low-priority customers after seizing the resource (see
set_prioritization), so that they can be preempted by high-priority
customers, but not by the closing process, and at the same time the
closing process has a higher priority than low-priority customers
*before* being served.

Hope it helps.

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I try to simulate a manufacturing process that works on the basis of pull, that is a new entity enters the process only if there is capacity to handle it. Imagine a press that is pulling material from a container: if the press is down, no material is pulled so no "product" enters the system..

My first idea, that works but it is not very elegant is to generate an unrealistically high number of entries and use a branch at the start of the trajectory to immediately reject the entity if there is no free capacity. I use the "get_server count" to see how many servers are busy and if all, then the entry is rejected.

This is quite wasteful in terms of computing, most of the time I just get entities thatflow  in and out of the system. Is there a more elegant way?

Basically the idea would be in pseudo_code like this:

        FOR(;;){
              WHILE (all systems busy) {
                     Do nothing
              }
            Generate new entry
        }

What I am doing instead is:

       FOR(once in a second){
          Generate new entry
          IF(system busy)
               Reject immediately
          ELSE
              Run trajectory
       }

Kind regards
Sandor

messages.subject_clean: resuming a timeout after a trap
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

There is a nice example on in the Bank Tutorial II (https://r-simmer.org/articles/simmer-04-bank-2.html) where a signal is handled while doing a timeout. The intention is to continue after handling the trap using the same timeout as before. The solution used is to record the start time and timeout value in attributes and use these to compute the time left for a new timeout() call at the end of handling the trap.

However, I am looking at a problem where the bank closes and before closing it sends a signal. The aim of the trap is to increase the priority of the arrival and then to continue with the timeout. However, in my case the resource is also preemptible so when subtracting the current time from the original end time (start_time + delay), end time might be too low since the arrival could have been preempted earlier.

Example:
arrive at 17:00, timeout is 2 hours
preemption by other arrival from 17:30-17:45
bank closes at 18:00 -> signal is sent.
trap computes remaining delay as  17:00 + 2 hours - 18:00 = 1 hour. This is incorrect since only 45 minutes were spent so the remaining time is 1:45.
Is there a way to get the current activity time in a trajectory? This way a similar computation can be done using
activity times and I can write an interuptible timeout method

Cheers
  Erik

I can think of at least on workaround, which would be to split the timeout into a number of equal parts and keep track of the remaining time. E.g. for a timeout of 5 I could use:

> set_attribute("remaining_time", 4.5) %>%
> timeout(1) %>%
> set_attribute("remaining_time", 3.5) %>%
> timeout(1) %>%
> set_attribute("remaining_time", 2.5) %>%
> timeout(1) %>%
> set_attribute("remaining_time", 1.5) %>%
> timeout(1) %>%
> set_attribute("remaining_time", 0.5) %>%
> timeout(1)

Then the remaining_time attribute can be used in the trap. DIsadvantage is that for a few arrivals there could be some inaccuracy in the timeout when the bank closes. However, the above code compensates that by estimating that on average the interruption will be in the middle of a time interval.

>     log_("Received notification that bank is closing") %>%

>     timeout(timeoutValue)
> }
>
> interruptibleTimeout = function(trajectory, timeoutValue) {
>   n = 100
>   trajectory = trajectory %>%
>      trap("closing", handler = bank_is_closing(timeoutValue/n/2))
>   for (i in 1:n) {
>     trajectory = trajectory %>%
>       timeout(timeoutValue/n)
>   }
>   trajectory %>% untrap("closing")
> }

Then use interruptibleTimeout instead of timeout.

messages.body_plain:
I am very new to simmer but familiar with R.  Thus far the package has been excellent in understanding the the front end of the apple packing operation.

I am trying to run a simluation whereby the basic units are apples.  These apples are graded and sorted by diameter (which I have done successfully - using multiple branches).  The next step is they enter a queue (accumulation) and get packaged into tubes (3,4 and 5 apples per tube depending on the size).  These are then packaged into shipping cartons (16 tubes per carton).  The cartons are palletised and the pallets loaded into shipping cartons.

My question is how do I trigger an arrival of a tube to shipping carton to pallet (128 cartons per pallet) and the shipping container (21 pallets per container) (I feel that using a if loop with a modulus approach would work but am unsure how to code it within a trajectory?)  I have attached my code below for reference.  Just a general approach to consolidated units would be useful for me at this stage.

Best regards
Stuart Dykes

library(simmer)

env <- simmer()

set.seed(1234)

traj <- trajectory() %>%
#
# assign a diameter as a trribute to each arrival
#
  set_attribute("diameter",function() rnorm(1,58.3,5.2)) %>%
#
# This intial branch partitions off the 15% rejects which go for juicing
#
  branch(
    option=function() sample(c(1, 2), 1, prob=c(0.85, 0.15)), continue=c(T,F),
    trajectory("export") %>%
      seize("INV_export",1) %>%
      timeout(function() (0.05)) %>%
      release("INV_export",1),
    trajectory("reject") %>%
      seize("INV_reject",1) %>%
      timeout(function() (0.05)) %>%
      release("INV_reject",1)
  ) %>%
#
# Send the apples to their appropriate drop based on their diameter
#
  branch(
    option= function() if(get_attribute(env,"diameter") >=71.6) 1 else 2, continue=c(T,T),
    trajectory("oversize_apples") %>%
      seize("os_packline",1) %>%
      timeout(function() rnorm(1, 0.8, .2)) %>%
      release("os_packline",1),
    trajectory("smaller_apples_1") %>%
      branch(
        function() if(get_attribute(env,"diameter") >=65.3) 1 else 2, continue=c(T,T),
        trajectory("72_tube_drop") %>%
          seize("72/4_packline",1) %>%
          timeout(function() rnorm(1, 0.8, .2)) %>%
          release("72/4_packline",1) %>%
          count72 <- count72 + 1,
        trajectory("smaller_apples_2") %>%
          branch(
            function() if(get_attribute(env,"diameter") >=60.8) 1 else 2, continue=c(T,T),
            trajectory("67_tube_drop") %>%
              seize("67/4/5_packline",1) %>%
              timeout(function() rnorm(1, 0.8, .2)) %>%
              release("67/4/5_packline",1),
            trajectory("smaller_apples_3") %>%
              branch(
                function() if(get_attribute(env,"diameter") >=59.6) 1 else 2, continue=c(T,T),
                trajectory("63/4_tube_drop") %>%
                  seize("63/4_packline",1) %>%
                  timeout(function() rnorm(1, 0.8, .2)) %>%
                  release("63/4_packline",1),
                trajectory("smaller_apples_4") %>%
                  branch(
                    function() if(get_attribute(env,"diameter") >=56.1) 1 else 2, continue=c(T,T),
                    trajectory("63/0/3/5T_tube_drop") %>%
                      seize("63/0/3/5T_packline",1) %>%
                      timeout(function() rnorm(1, 0.8, .2)) %>%
                      release("63/0/3/5T_packline",1),
                    trajectory("smaller_apples_5") %>%
                      branch(
                        function() if(get_attribute(env,"diameter") >=55) 1 else 2, continue=c(T,T),
                        trajectory("63/5_tube_drop") %>%
                          seize("63/5_packline",1) %>%
                          timeout(function() rnorm(1, 0.8, .2)) %>%
                          release("63/5_packline",1),
                        trajectory("smaller_apples_5") %>%
                          branch(
                            function() if(get_attribute(env,"diameter") >=50.6) 1 else 2, continue=c(T,T),
                            trajectory("58/5_tube_drop") %>%
                              seize("58/5_packline",1) %>%
                              timeout(function() rnorm(1, 0.8, .2)) %>%
                              release("58/5_packline",1),
                            trajectory("smaller_apples_6") %>%
                              branch(
                                function() if(get_attribute(env,"diameter") >=45.9) 1 else 2, continue=c(T,T),
                                trajectory("53/5_tube_drop") %>%
                                  seize("53/5_packline",1) %>%
                                  timeout(function() rnorm(1, 0.8, .2)) %>%
                                  release("53/5_packline",1),
                                trajectory("undersize_apples") %>%
                                  seize("us_packline",1) %>%
                                  timeout(function() rnorm(1, 0.8, .2)) %>%
                                  release("us_packline",1)
                              )
                          )
                      )
                  )
              )
          )
      )
  )
#
env %>%
#
  add_resource("os_packline",1) %>%
  add_resource("72/4_packline",1) %>%
  add_resource("67/4/5_packline",3) %>%
  add_resource("63/4_packline",1) %>%
  add_resource("63/0/3/5T_packline",4) %>%
  add_resource("63/5_packline",1) %>%
  add_resource("58/5_packline",2) %>%
  add_resource("53/5_packline",1) %>%
  add_resource("us_packline",1) %>%
#
  add_resource("INV_export", 1) %>%
  add_resource("INV_reject", 1) %>%
  add_generator("apple", traj, at(seq(0,100,by=0.0625)),mon=2)
#
env %>%
 run() %>% invisible

arrivals <- get_mon_arrivals(env, per_resource = T)
attribute <- get_mon_attributes(env)
resources <- get_mon_resources(env)

table(arrivals$resource)
#
capture.output(env)

If you use the simple generator "function() 1", one arrival is
generated every minute (if you are using minutes as the base time
unit). If you instead use "function() c(1, 0)", then one arrival is
generated in one minute and another one right afterwards (null
interarrival time), so 2 arrivals are generated every minute.

function() c(rnorm(1, 6), rep(0, rnorm(1, 4525)))

generates around 4525 arrivals approx. every 6 minutes. You can adjust
the standard deviations to fit your needs or even choose other
distributions.

Then it's clear that you don't need batching, but a kind of custom
priority queue that changes dynamically. I think that this can be
achieved with simmer, but requires a careful design. You'll need, at
least, the following elements:

1) Every arrival must have a private attribute establishing the type or class.

2) The first arrival that seizes the empty server must set its type as
a global attribute, meaning that this type of arrival is being
processed.

3) Then you need to "rotate" the whole queue: the next arrival enters
the server, and the type is checked (this is obviously a branch). If
the type is the same, it continues and proceeds to the timeout
function; otherwise, it must release immediately and be inserted into
the queue again. This happens until the server is full or the whole
queue has been checked ("rotated").

4) To be able to re-insert arrivals, you need to increase the priority
(so that they are inserted before eventual new arrivals) and then
simply roll back to the seize activity.

5) But they can't roll back straight away, because it would cause an
infinite loop. They need to wait there until the server is released
(the trap-wait-send mechanism is ideal for this).

In fact, on second thought, if you don't set a maximum capacity for
the resource and instead you control this through the check in step
3), then you don't need to increase the priority in step 4), because
you don't even need the queue at all.
